The network of arteries (LAD, RCA, Circumflex) supplying oxygenated blood to the heart muscle.
Tricuspid, Pulmonary, Mitral, and Aortic valves ensuring unidirectional blood flow.

interactive_questions.title: Conduction System Mapping
interactive_questions.prompt: Trace the electrical pathway of a normal heartbeat.
interactive_questions.question: Click the structure that acts as the 'Pacemaker' of the heart.
interactive_questions.explanation: The Sinoatrial (SA) Node initiates the electrical impulse, setting the pace for the heart.

theory.title: Cardiac Conduction
theory.content: The heart's pumping action is orchestrated by an intrinsic electrical system. The SA Node (Sinoatrial) generates the impulse, which travels through the atria to the AV Node (Atrioventricular). There is a slight delay here to allow the atria to contract fully. The signal then shoots down the Bundle of His and spreads through the Purkinje Fibers to contract the ventricles.
theory.analogy: The conduction system is like the electrical wiring of a house. The SA node is the main fuse box or 'master switch' that sends power to the lights (heart muscle). If the main fuse blows, backup generators (AV node) can kick in, but they are dimmer (slower heart rate).
theory.application: In 'Sick Sinus Syndrome', the SA node fails to fire reliably. We treat this by implanting a Pacemaker, which acts as an artificial fuse box to send regular electrical signals.

critical_concepts.elaboration: P wave (Atrial depolarization), QRS (Ventricular depolarization), T wave (Repolarization).
Identifying abnormal patterns like Atrial Fibrillation (irregularly irregular) or V-Tach (wide, fast).

interactive_questions.title: Arrhythmia Simulation
interactive_questions.prompt: Observe the live rhythm strip. Note the absence of P-waves and irregular R-R intervals.
interactive_questions.question: Diagnose the rhythm:
interactive_questions.explanation: The chaotic baseline (no defined P-waves) and irregular spacing between beats are hallmarks of AFib.

theory.title: Atrial Fibrillation
theory.content: AFib is caused by disorganized electrical signals in the atria. Instead of a strong, coordinated contraction, the atria quiver chaotically.
theory.analogy: Normal rhythm is like a well-drilled army marching in step. AFib is like a disorganized crowd running in all directions. The result is ineffective movement (blood flow) and chaos (irregular pulse).
theory.application: Because blood stagnates in the quivering atria, clots can form. If a clot travels to the brain, it causes a stroke. This is why AFib patients often need blood thinners (anticoagulants) to prevent strokes.

interactive_questions.title: Emergency Rhythm
interactive_questions.prompt: Patient is unresponsive. Monitor shows wide complexes at >150 bpm.
interactive_questions.question: Diagnose the rhythm:
interactive_questions.explanation: Wide, regular complexes at a rapid rate indicate V-Tach, a medical emergency.

theory.title: Ventricular Tachycardia
theory.content: V-Tach originates in the ventricles and causes them to beat extremely fast. This prevents the heart from filling with enough blood between beats, leading to a drastic drop in blood pressure.
theory.analogy: Imagine a car engine revving at maximum RPM while in neutral. It's working incredibly hard and making a lot of noise, but the car isn't moving anywhere. The heart is beating so fast it's effectively pumping nothing.
theory.application: Stable V-Tach can be treated with meds (Amiodarone). Unstable or pulseless V-Tach requires immediate electrical cardioversion or defibrillation to 'reset' the heart's electrical system.

critical_concepts.elaboration: The volume of blood in the ventricles at the end of diastole (stretching the muscle).
The resistance the heart must overcome to circulate blood (systemic vascular resistance).
Stroke Volume × Heart Rate. The total volume pumped per minute.

interactive_questions.title: Hemodynamic Controls
interactive_questions.prompt: Adjust the physiological parameters to observe changes in Blood Pressure and Cardiac Output.
interactive_questions.question: What happens to Blood Pressure when you significantly increase Afterload (Vasoconstriction)?
interactive_questions.explanation: Increasing afterload (tightening arteries) increases resistance, which raises blood pressure but forces the heart to work harder.

theory.title: Frank-Starling Law
theory.content: The Frank-Starling Law states that the heart pumps all the blood returned to it. Increased venous return (Preload) stretches the muscle fibers, leading to a stronger contraction.
theory.analogy: Think of the heart as a balloon. Preload is how much air you blow into it; the more you stretch it, the harder it snaps back. Afterload is like squeezing the neck of the balloon while letting air out; the tighter you squeeze (resistance), the harder it is for air to escape.
theory.application: In heart failure, the 'balloon' is overstretched and flabby. We give diuretics to lower preload (reduce the air) and ACE inhibitors to lower afterload (stop squeezing the neck), making it easier for the weak heart to pump.

critical_concepts.elaboration: Ultrasound of the heart to visualize valves, wall motion, and ejection fraction.
Using contrast dye and X-rays to visualize blockages in coronary arteries.

interactive_questions.title: Virtual Echocardiography
interactive_questions.prompt: Toggle between Normal and Dilated Cardiomyopathy views.
interactive_questions.question: In the 'Dilated' view, how does the left ventricle compare to normal?
options: Chamber is enlarged and walls are thin
interactive_questions.answer: Chamber is enlarged and walls are thin
interactive_questions.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by an enlarged LV cavity with thinned walls and reduced contractility.

theory.title: Echocardiogram Modes
theory.content: Echos allow us to see the heart beating in real-time. We assess Ejection Fraction (EF), which is the percentage of blood pumped out with each beat (Normal is 55-70%).
theory.analogy: An echocardiogram is like using a weather radar (sonar) to see inside a storm. Instead of rain clouds, we see moving blood and muscle walls using sound waves.
theory.application: Echo is the first-line test for Heart Failure. If a patient is short of breath, a quick Echo can tell us if the heart is pumping weakly (Systolic Failure) or if it's stiff and not filling properly (Diastolic Failure).

critical_concepts.elaboration: Highly specific proteins released into blood when heart muscle is damaged (MI).
Brain Natriuretic Peptide, released in response to ventricular stretch (Heart Failure).
Measures cholesterol (LDL, HDL) to assess long-term risk of atherosclerosis.

interactive_questions.title: Troponin Release Curve
interactive_questions.prompt: Analyze the biomarker release timeline after chest pain onset.
interactive_questions.question: Which biomarker rises first, and how long does Troponin stay elevated?
options: CK-MB rises first; Troponin stays ~1 week
interactive_questions.answer: CK-MB rises first; Troponin stays ~1 week
interactive_questions.explanation: Myoglobin rises earliest but is non-specific. Troponin rises within 3-4 hours and can remain elevated for 10-14 days, making it useful for late diagnosis.

theory.title: Cardiac Biomarkers
theory.content: Troponin I/T are the gold standards. CK-MB is useful for detecting re-infarction because it clears from the system faster (2-3 days).
theory.analogy: Imagine the heart muscle cells are filled with a specific red dye (Troponin). When the cell wall bursts due to injury (Heart Attack), that dye leaks into the river (bloodstream). By measuring the color of the river, we know if a dam broke upstream.
theory.application: We use 'serial troponins' to rule out a heart attack. One negative test isn't enough because the 'dye' takes a few hours to reach the testing site. We repeat the test every 3-6 hours to catch the rise.

critical_concepts.elaboration: Plaque buildup in arteries leading to stenosis and potential rupture.
Systolic (pumping problem) vs. Diastolic (filling problem) dysfunction.

interactive_questions.title: Coronary Artery Disease
interactive_questions.question: What is the immediate event that typically causes a heart attack (MI)?
interactive_questions.explanation: While narrowing causes angina, a heart attack is usually caused by the sudden rupture of a plaque, which triggers a blood clot that completely blocks the artery.

theory.title: The Ischemic Cascade
theory.content: Ischemia (lack of oxygen) leads to Injury, which if untreated leads to Infarction (tissue death). Time is muscle.
theory.analogy: Atherosclerosis is like a kitchen sink pipe slowly clogging with grease (plaque). A heart attack isn't just the slow clog—it's when a chunk of grease breaks off and completely plugs the drain instantly, causing an overflow (damage).
theory.application: Stents are like plumbing snakes used to clear the blockage. Statins are like using high-quality soap to prevent grease from sticking to the pipes in the first place.

critical_concepts.elaboration: Distinguishing between cardiac and non-cardiac causes of chest pain.
Using ECG to determine urgency of reperfusion.

interactive_questions.title: ER Case: 55M Chest Pain
interactive_questions.prompt: Patient presents with crushing chest pain. BP 160/90. ECG shows ST elevation in V1-V4.

patient.complaint: Crushing substernal pain, 10/10, radiating to left arm.

interactive_questions.question: What is the diagnosis and immediate action?
interactive_questions.explanation: ST elevation in anterior leads (V1-V4) indicates an Anterior STEMI. This requires immediate reperfusion therapy (PCI in Cath Lab).

theory.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome
theory.content: Management relies on MONA (Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin) and rapid reperfusion.
theory.analogy: A STEMI is like a house fire. You don't wait to schedule an inspection; you call the fire department (Cath Lab) immediately to put it out before the structure (heart muscle) collapses.
theory.application: Door-to-Balloon time is the key metric. We aim to open the blocked artery within 90 minutes of the patient hitting the ER door to save the heart muscle.

critical_concepts.elaboration: Slow heart rate and decrease contractility to reduce oxygen demand.
Lower blood pressure by preventing conversion of Angiotensin I to II.

interactive_questions.title: Mechanism of Action
interactive_questions.prompt: Drag the drug to the heart to see its effect on Vitals.
interactive_questions.question: Which drug effectively lowers Heart Rate?
interactive_questions.explanation: Beta blockers bind to beta-adrenergic receptors, blocking epinephrine/norepinephrine, which directly reduces heart rate and contractility.

theory.title: Cardiovascular Pharmacology
theory.content:
Beta Blockers (-olol): Reduce workload.
ACE Inhibitors (-pril): Vasodilate and reduce afterload.
Diuretics: Reduce preload/fluid.
theory.analogy: Beta blockers are like a governor on a car engine; they prevent the engine (heart) from revving too high, saving gas (oxygen). ACE Inhibitors widen the highway (arteries), so traffic (blood) flows smoother with less pressure.
theory.application: We start Beta Blockers after a heart attack to rest the heart. We start ACE Inhibitors in heart failure to prevent the heart from remodeling (changing shape) under high pressure.
